🐾 Matt’s payments work includes corporate payment engines, cross-border workflows, legacy-system migration, and developer integration.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, the ACCESS Next Generation program needed more than an out-of-box banking platform. Its **135,000+** clients across **180+ countries** required payment-specific formatting, validation, compliance, and approval workflows. Regional legacy systems also had different data models, entitlements, and transaction histories that had to move without interrupting live payments.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and bank resources. He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and government tax payment modules on Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform. The work included NACHA file validation, payment-type-specific entitlements, Message Authentication Code security, sanctions screening, and risk-based approval controls. He also owned on-call and critical incident response for the payment engine. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**; the payments migration completed **without disruption to live payment operations**, preserving compliance traceability.

At **American Express**, the Virtual Payments Platform’s adoption was slowed by missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, no sandbox, and testing dependencies. Matt led work on a developer portal, Java/.NET/Python SDKs, use case-driven API documentation, and a secure sandbox. He introduced environment virtualization and used Lean Product and XP practices. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, onboarding time fell, and the team exceeded its delivery commitment by **over 261 story points**.

At **RBC**, Matt designed cross-border payment workflows from initiation through settlement and reconciliation. He partnered with the FX team on real-time currency conversion, automated alerts, bulk processing, recurring payments, and Interac e-Transfer workflows. The work produced an implementation blueprint ready for development; revised payment cutoff processes reduced wire-transfer delays and improved SLA compliance.

🐾 There were production defects in the **JP Morgan Chase** payments work, including a Message Authentication Code (MAC) failure and legacy data issues after cutover.

The MAC security layer let corporate users validate payment integrity before release. A failure in that layer was traced to **missing unit tests and weak error handling**. Matt had break-glass production access and queried live payment data via SQL to triage the defect. The story identifies the root cause, but does not specify the outage duration, affected transaction count, or the exact corrective code changes.

During the migration, production defects also surfaced after cutover, primarily **data issues carried over from the legacy platform**. The regional systems had different schemas, formats, client configurations, entitlement structures, and compliance records. Moving them into a unified model did not eliminate every inherited data problem. Matt ran UAT and production validation/shakeout testing, then triaged the defects that emerged during rollout.

Across successive releases, waves, and migrations, Matt owned critical incident response and on-call accountability. He coordinated root-cause analysis across the bank’s New York team, offshore teams in Mumbai and Bangalore, and **Bottomline Technologies**. While incidents were live, he ran status updates and daily leadership calls.

The distinction is that **production defects occurred**, but the migration story reports **no disruption to live payment operations**. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**. There is no documented missed launch or quantified financial loss in these accounts.
